# Genesis 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter is a reaffirmation and expansion of the covenant God first announced in Genesis 12 and formalised in Genesis 15. After 13 years of divine silence (since Ishmael's birth, Gen 16:16), God appears to Abram at age 99, reveals Himself as **El Shaddai** (God Almighty), changes Abram's name to Abraham and Sarai's to Sarah, institutes circumcision as the covenant sign, and promises that Sarah herself will bear the covenant son, Isaac.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 1: *"When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said, 'I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless.'"*

- **The 13-year gap:** Abram was 86 when Ishmael was born (Gen 16:16); now he is 99. For 13 years there is no recorded word from God. Calvin suggests this silence was chastisement for Abram's hasty marriage to Hagar. Spurgeon noted, "All these thirteen years, so far as Scripture informs us, Abram had not a single visit from his God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary (Pulpit Commentary cited)

- **"The LORD appeared":** This is one of only a few definite appearance-visits from God to Abraham (others: Gen 12:7, 15:1 in vision, 18:1). Guzik suggests this was likely a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary

- **El Shaddai ("God Almighty"):** Scholars debate the etymology. Options include: (a) from *shadad* = "to be strong/powerful" (Keil, Leupold); (b) from *she-* + *day* = "who is sufficient" (Kidner, rabbinic view); (c) from *shad* = "breast," implying nourishment and tender care (Barnhouse); (d) from Akkadian *shadu* = "mountain," suggesting strength (Albright). The LXX translates it *pantokrator* — "the One who has His hand on everything." Delitzsch described El Shaddai as "the God who compels nature to do what is contrary to itself." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

- **"Walk before Me":** Literally "walk before My face" — a call to live *coram Deo*, conscious that God's eyes are always upon one. The phrase denotes the service due a king (Reformation Study Bible). It is a less intimate phrase than "walk with God" used of Enoch (Gen 5:24) and Noah (Gen 6:9), but still implies deep fellowship. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- **"Be blameless" (*tamim*):** Means "whole," "complete," "sound" — not sinless perfection but wholehearted devotion. The same word describes Noah (Gen 6:9) and unblemished sacrificial animals (Ex 12:5). The LXX translates it *amemptos* ("faultless"). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 2: *"I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly."*

- **"Establish" (lit. "give"):** This is not a new or additional covenant but the execution and confirmation of the one already made in Genesis 15. The Pulpit Commentary rejects the critical view that this is a different tradition (the "Elohist" narrative). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html

- **"I will multiply you exceedingly":** Repeats and intensifies the original promise (Gen 12:2; 13:16; 15:5). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## vv. 3–4: *"Then Abram fell facedown, and God said to him, 'As for Me, this is My covenant with you: You will be the father of many nations.'"*

- **"Fell facedown":** An act of reverential awe and worship (cf. Gen 24:52; Num 16:22). In v. 3 the name shifts: the LORD (v. 1), God Almighty (v. 1), and now Elohim (v. 3) — three divine names in three verses, underscoring the weight of the moment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary

- **"As for Me":** The emphatic Hebrew *'ani* (I Myself) stands at the head of the sentence. God takes the initiative. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- **"Father of many nations":** More than just Israel — this looks ahead to Ishmaelites, Edomites, descendants of Keturah, and, climactically, all believers (Rom 4:17; Gal 3:7–9). The Geneva Study Bible notes: "Not only physical descendants, but of a far greater multitude by faith." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 5: *"No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations."*

- **Abram → Abraham:** "Abram" means "exalted father" or "high father"; "Abraham" means "father of a multitude" (popular etymology, not strictly scientific). The name change is a seal confirming God's promise. Guzik notes the irony: a childless man now bears the name "father of many nations" — faith bearing an uncomfortable name. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html

- **"I have made you":** The perfect tense — God speaks of what He has already determined as though it were already accomplished. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- **Name changes in Scripture:** God also renamed Jacob → Israel (Gen 32:28), Simon → Peter (Mark 3:16), and promises a new name to every overcomer (Rev 2:17). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## v. 6: *"I will make you exceedingly fruitful; I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you."*

- The promises are expanded beyond what was stated in Genesis 12: multiple nations and kings (e.g., David, Solomon, and ultimately the Messiah) are now explicitly promised. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary lists the Ishmaelites, descendants of Keturah, Edomites, and Israelites as fulfilments of "nations." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

---

## v. 7: *"I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, to be your God and the God of your descendants after you."*

- **"Everlasting covenant" (*berit 'olam*):** Literally "a covenant of eternity." The phrase points to a covenant that spans generations, not that every individual inherits it automatically; faith is required. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- **"To be God to you":** A formula comprehending all saving benefits — a clear indication of the spiritual character of the Abrahamic covenant (cf. Heb 11:16). This becomes standard covenant language throughout the OT (Ex 6:7; Lev 26:12; Jer 31:33). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 8: *"And to you and your descendants I will give the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan—as an eternal possession; and I will be their God."*

- **"The land of your sojournings":** Abraham lived as a "stranger" (sojourner) in Canaan; he never owned it in his lifetime except a burial cave (Gen 23). The promise looks beyond his lifetime. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

- **"Everlasting possession":** The Pulpit Commentary explains that the earthly Canaan would remain with Abraham's descendants so long as they kept the covenant conditions, while the heavenly Canaan is the inheritance of Abraham's spiritual children. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pulpit/genesis/17.htm

- **Denominational note — Dispensational vs. Covenant Theology:** Dispensationalists see this land promise as an unconditional, literal, future promise to ethnic Israel yet to be fully fulfilled. Covenant theologians see it fulfilled in Christ — the land typologically points to the new creation, and the Church (Jew and Gentile in Christ) inherits the promise in a spiritual/eschatological sense. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/podcasts/help-me-teach-the-bible/ligon-duncan-covenant-theology-dispensationalism/

---

## v. 9: *"God also said to Abraham, 'You must keep My covenant—you and your descendants in the generations after you.'"*

- **"You must keep My covenant":** The covenant has a human-responsibility side. The Reformation Study Bible notes: "The covenant relationship between God and Abraham includes both promises obligating God to Abraham (Gen 17:4–8, 16), and commands obligating Abraham and Sarah to God ('As for you,' Gen 17:9–15)." This is not a contract of equals but a sovereignly bestowed covenant that calls for obedient response. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-17-commentary ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 10: *"This is My covenant with you and your descendants after you, which you are to keep: Every male among you must be circumcised."*

- The Geneva Study Bible notes that circumcision is called "the covenant" because it signifies the covenant and has the promise of grace joined to it — a phrase common to all ordinances. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html

- **Not unique to Israel:** Circumcision was practised among several ancient Near Eastern peoples. What made Israel's practice distinctive was its timing (eighth day, not at puberty) and its meaning (covenant sign, not merely a rite of passage). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## v. 11: *"You are to circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you."*

- **Why the foreskin?** The Geneva Bible notes: "That private part is circumcised, to show that all that is begotten by man is corrupt, and must die." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html

- Ellicott comments that circumcision represents "a new birth by the putting off of the old man, and the dedication of the new man unto holiness. The flesh was cast away that the spirit might grow strong." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/17.htm

- Spurgeon: "Circumcision indicated to the seed of Abraham that there was a defilement of the flesh in man which must for ever be taken away, or man would remain impure, and out of covenant with God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

- Guzik notes it was also associated with the reproductive organ because the covenant promise concerned the special "seed" of Abraham that would ultimately bring the Messiah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## v. 12: *"Generation after generation, every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner—even those who are not your offspring."*

- **Eighth day:** Ellicott explains this is "just one week after birth, as the day of birth was counted among the eight days." Modern medicine has confirmed that vitamin K (needed for blood clotting) is at inadequate levels until days 5–7, and prothrombin peaks on day 8 — making it the safest, earliest day for the procedure. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/17.htm

- **Household principle:** The covenant sign was not limited to biological descendants. Slaves and foreigners in the household were included. This is a "household principle" rather than a strict "genealogical principle." — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-abrahamic-covenant-in-reformed-baptist-perspective/

---

## v. 13: *"Whether they are born in your household or purchased, they must be circumcised. My covenant in your flesh will be an everlasting covenant."*

- The double mention ("born in your house or bought with money") emphasises the comprehensive scope — no male in the household was exempt. This reinforces that ethnicity was not determinative for inclusion in the covenant community. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-abrahamic-covenant-in-reformed-baptist-perspective/

- **"In your flesh":** The covenant sign was physically inscribed on the body — an irreversible mark of belonging. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 14: *"But if any male is not circumcised, he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant."*

- **"Cut off":** The same Hebrew verb used for "cutting" a covenant (Gen 15:10). Here in the Niphal stem it denotes the death penalty or excommunication. Disobedience had the most serious consequences. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html

- The Geneva Bible notes: "Though women were not circumcised, they still partook of God's promise: for under mankind all was consecrated. Here it is declared, that whoever condemns the sign, also despises the promise." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html

---

## v. 15: *"Then God said to Abraham, 'As for Sarai your wife, do not call her Sarai, for her name is to be Sarah.'"*

- **Sarai → Sarah:** Both names derive from the root meaning "princess," but "Sarai" (my princess) confines dominion to one family, while "Sarah" (princess) is absolute — "princess of a multitude" (Poole). The added *he* letter in Hebrew identifies her relationship to Yahweh in the covenant of grace, just as it did in Abraham's name change. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 16: *"And I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she will be the mother of nations; kings of peoples will descend from her."*

- **"By her":** The emphasis falls on "her" — God makes it unmistakably clear that the promised son will come through Sarah herself, not through a surrogate (as with Hagar). Sarah is now explicitly included in the covenant promises. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html

- **"Mother of nations; kings":** The same language used of Abraham (v. 6) is now applied to Sarah — she shares equally in the dignity of the promise. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 17: *"Abraham fell facedown. Then he laughed and said to himself, 'Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah give birth at the age of ninety?'"*

- **"Fell facedown" then "laughed":** Note the distinction between outward act (reverence) and inner reaction. Only God sees both. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

- **What kind of laughter?** Traditional interpretation (Geneva Bible, Guzik, Garner-Howes) sees this as laughter of joyous amazement, not cynical doubt. The Geneva Bible states: "Which proceeded from a sudden joy, and not from lack of faith." Romans 4:19–21 confirms Abraham "did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

- However, some (Calvin) see an element of weakness or struggle in Abraham's faith here, noting that even great faith can coexist with momentary incredulity at the sheer impossibility of the promise. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

- **"A hundred years old…ninety":** Abraham's own testimony underscores the biological impossibility — both are "as good as dead" regarding childbearing (Rom 4:19; Heb 11:12). This sets the stage for a miracle of resurrection power. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## v. 18: *"And Abraham said to God, 'O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!'"*

- This is Abraham's plea — perhaps a last attempt to "help" God fulfil the promise through the son he already has, or an expression of genuine fatherly love for Ishmael. Calvin reads it negatively, as a lingering lack of faith. Garner-Howes sees it as evidence of Abraham's love for Ishmael and his desire that Ishmael share in covenant blessings. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html

---

## v. 19: *"But God replied, 'Your wife Sarah will indeed bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac. I will establish My covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him.'"*

- **"Isaac" (*yitschaq*):** Means "he laughs" — an onomatopoeic name that would forever remind Abraham (and Sarah) of their laughter. Yet God transforms Sarah's later laughter of unbelief (Gen 18:12–15) into the laughter of joy at Isaac's birth (Gen 21:6). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-17.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

- **Covenant through Isaac, not Ishmael:** God makes an irrevocable choice — the covenant line runs through the child of promise, not the child of human effort (cf. Gal 4:22–31). The Geneva Bible: "The everlasting covenant is made with the children of the Spirit. A temporary promise is made with the children of the flesh, as was promised to Ishmael." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html

---

## v. 20: *"As for Ishmael, I have heard you, and I will surely bless him; I will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation."*

- **God hears Abraham:** The name "Ishmael" itself means "God hears." God answers Abraham's prayer, though not in the way Abraham hoped. Ishmael receives material blessing — twelve princes (listed in Gen 25:12–16) and nationhood — but not the covenant. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## v. 21: *"But I will establish My covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year."*

- **"At this time next year":** A specific, testable prophecy. The fulfilment would confirm that God alone performed what was humanly impossible. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

- **The covenant distinction is sharp:** Ishmael is blessed — greatly — but the *covenant* belongs to Isaac. This distinction drives much of the subsequent narrative and Paul's allegory in Galatians 4. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-abrahamic-covenant-in-reformed-baptist-perspective/

---

## v. 22: *"When He had finished speaking with Abraham, God went up from him."*

- **"Went up":** The idiom may simply mean God departed or "left suddenly." In the cultural conception of the ancient Near East, deity was thought to dwell above, so departing is described as "going up" (cf. Gen 11:5; 35:13). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

---

## v. 23: *"On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his household or purchased with his money—every male among the members of Abraham's household—and he circumcised them, just as God had told him."*

- **"That very same day":** Abraham's obedience was immediate. Guzik highlights three qualities: it was **complete** (every male), **prompt** (that very day), and **daring** (disabling all his fighting men at once — Abraham had 318 trained men, Gen 14:14). He didn't pray about it, ease into it, or delay — "God said it, and he did it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

- The Geneva Bible notes: "They were well taught if they obeyed and were circumcised without resistance. This teaches that masters in their houses ought to be as preachers to their families." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/genesis-17.html

---

## vv. 24–27: *"So Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, and his son Ishmael was thirteen; Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised on the same day. And all the men of Abraham's household—both servants born in his household and those purchased from foreigners—were circumcised with him."*

- **Abraham at 99, Ishmael at 13:** The ages are carefully recorded. For Ishmael, circumcision at 13 corresponds to the Arab custom of performing it at puberty — perhaps the origin of that practice. For Israelites, the command was the eighth day, marking it as a sign of covenant membership, not a puberty rite. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-17

- **"All the men":** The repetition emphasises the totality of obedience — none were exempted, none refused. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-17/

---

## Denominational Differences on Genesis 17 (especially vv. 9–14)

### Circumcision and Baptism

This is the major point of Protestant disagreement arising from this chapter:

**Reformed Paedobaptist (Presbyterian, Continental Reformed, some Anglicans and Lutherans):** See a direct continuity between circumcision and baptism. As circumcision was the sign of entrance into the old covenant community given to infant males, so baptism is the sign of entrance into the new covenant community given to infants of believers. Colossians 2:11–12 is read as explicitly connecting the two. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/does-baptism-replace-circumcision-an-examination-of-the-relationship-betwee/

**Reformed Baptist / Credobaptist:** Affirm the overarching unity of the covenant of grace but insist that the new covenant is not a mixed community (believers and unbelievers) as the old covenant was. In the new covenant, "they shall all know Me" (Jer 31:34). Therefore the sign (baptism) belongs only to those who give evidence of regeneration — the "household of faith," not the physical household. The genealogical principle of the old covenant gives way to the spiritual principle of the new. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-abrahamic-covenant-in-reformed-baptist-perspective/

**Dispensational:** Sees the Abrahamic covenant (including circumcision) as made with ethnic Israel, distinct from the Church. The land and nation promises to Abraham's physical seed remain to be literally fulfilled for Israel. The Church is not the fulfilment of these promises but a distinct entity in God's plan. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/podcasts/help-me-teach-the-bible/ligon-duncan-covenant-theology-dispensationalism/

**Lutheran:** Typically paedobaptist, seeing baptism as God's work in which He gives saving grace. The continuity between circumcision and baptism is affirmed, though Lutheran theology emphasises that baptismal grace must be received by faith. — https://www.lcms.org (not directly fetched, but standard Lutheran position noted from the specified source list)

### The Nature of the Covenant

- **Reformed / Covenant Theology:** Emphasises the unity of the covenant of grace across all administrations. Abraham's covenant is one unfolding stage of the one covenant of grace fulfilled in Christ.
- **Dispensational:** Emphasises the distinctiveness of each dispensation/administration. The Abrahamic covenant contains unconditional promises to ethnic Israel that are not transferred to the Church.
- **Methodist / Wesleyan:** Generally affirms covenant theology in a modified (non-Reformed) form, emphasising the conditional aspect ("walk before Me and be blameless") as underscoring the genuine human response required — synergism rather than monergism.
- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (e.g., Guzik/Enduring Word):** Reads the passage with emphasis on faith's obedience and God's miraculous power (the miraculous birth through Sarah prefigures God doing the impossible). The laughter of Abraham is read positively, as faith mixed with joyful amazement.
